chapters.title: Chapter 6: TCS and Putting It All Together

lessons.title: Common TDS Mistakes Individuals Make and How to Avoid Them

body.text: Almost every TDS problem an individual faces is self-inflicted and preventable: a declaration not made, a form not submitted, a PAN not linked, a statement never opened. None of it requires expertise. It requires a routine.

children.text: You have now seen TDS on salary, interest, dividends, fees, rent, property, crypto and winnings, plus the tools to reduce it and the process to claim it back. This lesson collects the ten mistakes that cost ordinary taxpayers the most, with the numbers attached, and turns them into a calendar you can actually follow.

body.caption: What they cost and how to avoid them

cells: Treating TDS as your final tax
A large bill at filing, plus interest under Sections 424 and 425. On ₹2,40,000 of FD interest in the 30% slab, ₹50,880 is still due after 10% TDS
Estimate your real tax at your slab rate and pay advance tax
Not telling payroll about other income
A year-end shortfall you did not plan for
Declare other income and TDS to your employer through Form 122
Reporting income net of TDS
A mismatch notice, because the payer reported the gross amount
Always report gross income and claim the TDS separately
Never opening your tax credit statement
Lost credits you discover years later
Check Form 168 (formerly Form 26AS and AIS) at least twice a year
Claiming credits with status U or O
The credit is disallowed and a demand follows
Claim only final credits, and chase the deductor for the rest
Not submitting Form 121 when eligible
Refunds you wait a year for. A senior with ₹4,80,000 of interest loses the use of ₹48,000
Submit Form 121 to each payer every April if you qualify
Submitting Form 121 when you do not qualify
A false declaration, with prosecution risk under Section 482
Apply both tests honestly, and use a Section 395 certificate instead
Letting your PAN go inoperative
TDS at 20% instead of 10%, and refunds withheld. On ₹3,00,000 of fees, ₹30,000 extra
Check Link Aadhaar Status today and fix it for ₹1,000
Changing jobs without Form 122
Both employers under-deduct. A mid-year switch can leave ₹97,500 unpaid, plus about ₹8,820 of interest
Give the new employer your previous salary and TDS details
Forgetting that you are a deductor
Interest and fees on rent, property and contractor payments. A tenant who ignores 2% on ₹60,000 rent faces about ₹15,696 of interest and fees
Check the rules before paying rent above ₹50,000 a month or buying property

body.title: What four of these mistakes cost in a single year

markDefs.definition: The gap between your actual tax for the year and the TDS and other taxes already paid. If it exceeds ₹10,000, advance tax was due, and interest applies.

children.text: The first mistake is the most common of all: assuming that because tax was deducted, the matter is closed. TDS rates are flat. Your tax is not. The difference is your
, and once it crosses ₹10,000 the interest clock starts running.

body.title: Try It: The 10% Illusion
body.prompt: A doctor in the 30% slab earns ₹2,40,000 of FD interest. The bank deducts 10%. Including 4% cess, how much tax does she still owe on that interest?
body.explanation: Her tax is ₹2,40,000 × 30% × 1.04 = ₹74,880. The bank deducted ₹24,000. The shortfall of ₹50,880 is hers to pay, and because it is far above ₹10,000, it should have gone out as advance tax during the year.

children.text: The second is the quiet one: becoming a deductor without realising it. A salaried tenant paying ₹60,000 a month must deduct 2% once a year, which is ₹14,400. Ignore it and the interest and late fee can cost more than the tax itself.

body.caption: A tenant who forgot, six months late

cells: TDS that should have been deducted from March rent
Interest at 1.5% a month for six months, Section 398
Late fee at ₹200 a day, capped at the TDS amount, Section 427
Total extra cost on top of the tax

body.title: Quick Check: The Expensive Habit
body.question: Which of these actually reduces the tax you pay for the year, rather than just delaying or rearranging it?
options: Splitting fixed deposits across several banks so no bank crosses the TDS threshold
Choosing the regime and deductions that produce the lower tax on your income
Asking your employer to deduct less TDS each month
body.explanation: Splitting deposits, Form 121 and lower salary TDS all change when tax is collected, not how much you owe. Only the regime and deduction choices in Chapter 2 change the tax itself. Keeping those two ideas separate is the single most useful habit in this course.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: Report It Gross
body.textWithBlank: If a client pays you ₹90,000 after deducting ₹10,000 of TDS, the income you report in your return is ₹___.
body.explanation: You report the gross ₹1,00,000 and separately claim the ₹10,000 as tax already paid. Reporting only what hit your bank understates income against what the client reported, which is one of the most common mismatch triggers.

children.text: Your TDS Year in Four Dates

body.title: A routine that prevents almost all of it

events.title: Set up the year
events.description: Choose your regime and tell payroll. Submit Form 121 to banks and companies if you qualify. Apply for a Section 395 certificate if TDS will far exceed your tax. Check that your PAN is operative.

events.title: Check and file
events.description: Reconcile last year's statement, chase missing credits, then file and e-verify your return. Pay any balance tax.

events.title: Advance tax checkpoints
events.description: Re-estimate income from interest, capital gains, rent and freelancing. Pay advance tax instalments if your shortfall after TDS will exceed ₹10,000.

events.title: Proofs and corrections
events.description: Submit investment proofs through Form 124 if you are in the old regime, and give payroll any other income or TDS details through Form 122.

body.title: Scenario: A Year of Small Oversights
body.scenario: Naveen, 41, in Coimbatore, changed jobs in October, kept ₹12,00,000 in fixed deposits across two banks, rented a flat at ₹55,000 a month, and never opened his tax credit statement. In June he finds a demand notice waiting, and his refund from the previous year was adjusted against it.
body.prompt: List what probably went wrong and what he should do now, in order.
body.modelAnswer: Four things likely went wrong. First, he did not give his new employer a Form 122, so both employers applied the standard deduction and the lower slabs separately and under-deducted. Second, his FD interest crossed the threshold at one or both banks, and 10% TDS would not cover his slab rate. Third, as a tenant paying above ₹50,000 a month he was required to deduct 2% once a year through Form 141, which he probably missed, exposing him to interest and a late fee. Fourth, by never checking his statement he could not see any of this coming. Now, in order: open the statement and reconcile it; respond to the demand on the portal rather than ignoring it, checking whether it arises from a genuine shortfall or from a credit that was disallowed; pay any genuine shortfall quickly to stop interest; deduct and deposit the rent TDS with interest and issue the landlord a Form 132; and set up the April routine so next year starts clean. None of these is difficult. All of them are expensive to postpone.

body.title: The Ten-Minute Annual Review
steps: Confirm your PAN is operative and linked with Aadhaar
List every source of income and the TDS rate that applies to it
Compare expected TDS with your expected tax, and decide between advance tax, Form 121 or a Section 395 certificate
Tell payroll about other income, other TDS and TCS, and any previous employer, using Form 122
Check that you are not an accidental deductor on rent, property or large contractor payments
Open your tax credit statement, reconcile it, and chase anything missing well before the filing deadline

body.label: Income Tax e-Filing Portal
body.description: One login covers most of this routine: Link Aadhaar Status, the Annual Information Statement, the tax calculator, e-Pay Tax for advance tax, and your return.

points: TDS is a prepayment at a flat rate, never proof that your tax is settled. Compare it with your real tax every year
Most costly mistakes are omissions: no Form 122 on a job switch, no Form 121 when eligible, no Aadhaar link, no look at the statement
Report income gross and claim TDS separately, and claim only credits shown as final
Watch for the moment you become a deductor yourself, on rent above ₹50,000 a month or a property purchase of ₹50 lakh or more
Splitting deposits or reducing TDS changes timing, not the tax. Only regime and deduction choices change what you owe
An April setup, a mid-year check, advance tax at the quarterly dates and a June reconciliation prevent almost every problem in this course
